uses: Sage is traditionally a mouth and throat herb: a strong infusion was gargled for a sore throat, mouth ulcers and bleeding gums, and fresh leaves were rubbed on the teeth. In folk practice sage tea was taken for a weak digestion and to calm night sweats, and nursing mothers used it to slow their milk when weaning. A cooled rinse was combed through the hair to darken it. Culpeper and many after him praised it for the memory. It is also a classic seasoning for pork, poultry stuffing and cheese.
taste: Warm, bitter and a little astringent
energetics: Culpeper called sage hot and dry in the second or third degree
caution_pregnancy: Sage may be unsafe in pregnancy because it contains thujone; NCCIH advises talking to your provider first, and the EMA does not recommend medicinal sage in pregnancy or breastfeeding. While nursing, note that sage is traditionally used to reduce milk supply. Not enough is known about safety for nursing babies; avoid medicinal amounts.
caution_medications: The EMA reports no known interactions, but few studies have looked. NCCIH advises anyone on medicines to talk with their provider before using herbal products.
caution_conditions: Sage contains thujone and camphor, which harm the nervous system in large amounts. Very high intake, especially of sage essential oil, has caused seizures, along with dizziness, a hot flushed feeling and a racing heart. Use isn't established for anyone under 18. Occasional side effects include wheezing, agitation, an upset or painful stomach and dizziness.
caution_duration: Food amounts are likely safe, and larger amounts have been used safely in studies for up to 8 weeks, but high amounts or long use may be unsafe because of thujone. If mouth or throat symptoms last more than a week, or digestive or skin complaints more than 2 weeks, see a practitioner.
caution_topical: Allergic reactions are possible; the EMA lists hypersensitivity as a reason not to use it. Never take sage essential oil by mouth; the EMA links it to seizures.
garden_harvest_timing: Pick leaves before the plant flowers. Cut back the top 6 to 8 inches at least twice a season, never taking more than half the plant.
garden_water: Tolerates drought but grows better with steady water; needs good drainage
notes: A short-lived woody perennial; replace or divide plants every few years when they turn leggy. Grows from seed or from cuttings and layering. Bees, butterflies and sometimes hummingbirds visit the flowers. Grieve records the old saying that eating sage in May brings long life, and the belief that the plant thrives or fails with its owner's fortunes. The name comes from Latin words for health and saving.
